passage: I've lived next door to Leela since we were six, so I know her family well. I'm Zainab. Her father is proud of her, really proud. Every test mark goes onto the family group within minutes. At dinner the talk is ranks, olympiads, which coaching batch next. When she got 94 in maths, he asked, "Who got the extra marks?" Last month on the terrace, Leela said, very quietly, "If I stop being clever, I think they'd stop liking me." I didn't know what to say. I just sat next to her. Then something changed. Her aunt must have said something. On Sunday I heard her father through the wall asking Leela to teach him the song she'd been humming. No marks, just singing badly together. Leela was laughing, properly laughing.

qa.q: Where does Leela's father post every test mark?
qa.a: Onto the family group within minutes.

qa.q: What was Leela afraid of, based on what she said on the terrace?
qa.a: She was afraid her family would stop liking her if she stopped being clever.

qa.q: What small change seemed to help Leela at home?
qa.a: Her father spent time singing with her with no talk of marks, showing interest in her beyond her ability.

qa.q: How does Zainab seem to feel watching Leela's situation?
qa.a: Zainab seems worried and unsure what to say, but stays close, and is glad to hear Leela laughing on Sunday.

grounding: A neighbour sees a gifted girl whose proud father pushes constant achievement until she feels loved only for being clever, and how valuing her beyond ability helps.

passage: Saturday. At his cousin's wedding, Yogesh put an arm around Gopika and told every uncle, "Our genius. Ninety-eight in science!" Gopika smiled until her cheeks hurt. Wednesday. The results came. Second rank. She went straight to the bathroom and cried with the tap running. When she came out she asked, "Papa, would you still love me if I was just ordinary?" Yogesh stared at her. He didn't answer. He hadn't known she thought that. The next Sunday. He took her for cutting chai at the corner stall. "I watched you with your little cousin at the wedding," he said. "You carried her when she was scared of the band. That's what I'm proudest of." He never mentioned the rank. Gopika leaned her head on his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Yogesh tell every uncle at the wedding?
qa.a: Our genius. Ninety-eight in science!

qa.q: What does Gopika's question to her father show she was worried about?
qa.a: It shows she worried his love depended on her marks and brilliance.

qa.q: What turning point did Yogesh choose after hearing her question?
qa.a: He took her for chai and praised her kindness to her cousin, not mentioning the rank at all.

qa.q: What was the wedding like for Gopika while Yogesh boasted?
qa.a: She smiled until her cheeks hurt, feeling shown off for her marks rather than just being herself.

grounding: It shows a proud father pushing achievement, a daughter who feels loved only for brilliance, and how valuing her beyond ability comforts her.

passage: After I won the state quiz at thirteen, Baba lined up all my trophies in the drawing room, where every guest could see them. Every dinner was about the next rank. When I got 88 in chemistry, Baba didn't shout. He just went quiet for two days. That silence hurt more than anything. I started thinking that I was only worth loving when I won. One night I told him, shaking, "Baba, do you like me, or just the trophies?" His face changed. He took me for a long walk by the lake and said, "I love you, Bidisha. Not the trophies." Now on Sundays we cycle, and we have a rule: nobody mentions marks. I still work hard. I just don't feel afraid any more.

qa.q: What mark did Bidisha get in chemistry?
qa.a: Bidisha got 88 in chemistry.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel during Baba's two days of silence?
qa.a: Bidisha felt deeply hurt and afraid, believing love came only with winning.

qa.q: What change helped protect Bidisha's well-being?
qa.a: Baba said clearly that he loved Bidisha, not the trophies, and they started Sunday cycling with a rule of no talk about marks.

qa.q: How might Baba have felt when asked if he liked the trophies more?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and sad to learn his pride had made his child feel loved only for winning.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose proud parent pushes constant achievement, who feels loved only for brilliance, and how valuing the child beyond ability protects well-being.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11, Wednesday.
Jeevan came in today saying he had not slept. He topped the pre-board but his mother asked why the maths was 97, not 100. He said, "Mum only smiles when I win something." He plays guitar in the school band, but she calls it a waste of revision time.
I asked his permission to call his mother in. She came this afternoon. When I read her his words, she cried and said she was only proud of him. We talked about how he hears it. We agreed on one evening a week with no talk of marks, and she said she would come to the band's performance on Saturday.
Next: check in with Jeevan on Monday. — Mehak

qa.q: What did Jeevan get in maths in the pre-board?
qa.a: He got 97 in maths.

qa.q: How does Jeevan feel about his mother's pride?
qa.a: He feels anxious and unloved except when winning, saying his mum only smiles when he wins something.

qa.q: What steps did Mehak take to help Jeevan?
qa.a: Mehak asked Jeevan's permission, met his mother, shared how he hears her pride and agreed a weekly evening with no talk of marks.

qa.q: How did Jeevan's mother react to hearing his words?
qa.a: She was hurt and shocked, crying and saying she was only proud of him, then agreed to value him beyond marks.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose proud parent pushes constant achievement so he feels loved only for results, and how valuing him beyond ability helps.

passage:
Sunday
Relatives over for lunch. Papa told everyone I'll crack the top engineering exam, "no question." He said it three times. Chacha asked what I like doing and I didn't know what to say.
Later Thomas came over and we were laughing at his cartoon of our physics sir. Papa came in and said, "No time for friends this year." Thomas left in two minutes.
I sat in my room and cried. I wanted to shout: am I just a rank to you? 
Then at night Papa knocked. He saw my face. He sat on the bed and said, "I've been so proud I forgot to ask about you. What do you like?" I said drawing. He got out my old sketchbook from the loft. We looked at it together till eleven.
Pradeep

qa.q: What did Papa take out from the loft?
qa.a: He got out Pradeep's old sketchbook from the loft.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel after Thomas left?
qa.a: Pradeep felt hurt and trapped, crying and wondering if Papa saw only a rank.

qa.q: What did Papa do at night that protected Pradeep's well-being?
qa.a: He admitted he forgot to ask about Pradeep, asked what Pradeep likes and spent time looking at the sketchbook together.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt being sent away?
qa.a: Thomas may have felt awkward and unwelcome, and perhaps worried about his friend.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose proud parent pushes for constant achievement, making love feel tied to rank, and a parent who begins valuing the child beyond ability.

passage:
Mum: Physics result? 🤔
Sachin: 92
Mum: What happened to the other 8? Riya's son got 99. You're capable of more.
Sachin: ok
Mum: We'll add Sunday tuition.
Sachin: Mum can I ask something
Mum: Yes
Sachin: Would you still be proud of me if I was just normal? Like 70s?
Sachin: Sometimes it feels like you only like me when I top.
Mum: ...
Mum: Sachin, that's not true. But I can see why it feels that way.
Mum: I'm sorry. I love you for you. Your jokes, how you help Nani with her phone, all of it.
Sachin: really?
Mum: Really. 92 is great. No Sunday tuition. Let's get chaat tonight.
Sachin: ok. thanks Mum

qa.q: Whose son got 99, according to Mum?
qa.a: Riya's son.

qa.q: How was Sachin feeling when asking if Mum would still be proud with marks in the 70s?
qa.a: Sachin felt hurt and anxious, as if Mum's love depended on being brilliant.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what did Mum do to fix it?
qa.a: Her pressure made Sachin feel loved only for marks; she apologised, named things she loves about Sachin beyond ability and dropped the extra tuition.

qa.q: How might Mum be feeling after reading Sachin's question?
qa.a: She seems shocked and guilty, then tender, realising her pride had come across as conditional love.

grounding: Sachin feels loved only for brilliance because of Mum's push for achievement, and her valuing Sachin beyond ability brings reassurance.
